docs.title: Structure diagram
docs.text:
The core and its MMU are unchanged from core_mmu. Below the MMU sits a bridge, which reads the physical address of each access and sends it either to main memory or to the peripheral devices (Timer, Serial, Interrupt Controller). The devices are one shared set on the memory side, not part of the core, the same way the AJIT processor organizes them. That is what lets several cores share them later.

Every arrow between modules is a net, and every net crossing costs at least one cycle. A memory access crosses four nets here (core to bridge to memory, and back), two more than in core_mmu. The Interrupt Controller sends its interrupt level to the core over its own net, as a level: a token arrives only when the level changes, and the core polls that net once per cycle. An interrupt therefore reaches the core one cycle after the Interrupt Controller raises it.

The devices' behavior is the same C++ class in both models (PeripheralDevicesCore). The cpp_model ticks it once after every core cycle. The sitar_model's PeripheralDevices module ticks it once per simulated cycle. See Peripheral Devices for what the devices do.

The same system as core_mmu_devices, with one more procedure inside Core: the split L1 caches, between sparcThread and mmu. docs.title: Performance Modeling
docs.text:
Model configuration knobs are of two kinds, structural and timing. See Model Configuration Settings for the complete list of both kinds, and where to set each one.

Once you've chosen knob values to model a specific system (rebuild first if any of them are compile-time), run the simulation with --stats enabled.

docs.title: Printing the performance measures
docs.text:
Every configuration's own executable, both drivers, takes an optional --stats flag, alongside the existing <hex_file> [expected_file] [max_cycles] arguments (it can appear anywhere among them):

model/system_models/core_mmu/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_mmu <hex> --stats

Off by default, so run_simple_test.sh and validation/run_tests.py run unaffected. When given, it prints every performance measure the model tracks (the table below), to stdout, once the run finishes. Each configuration prints only what it actually has: core_only prints its core statistics alone. core_mmu prints core statistics, then MMU statistics, then physical memory statistics.

In core_only, the core connects directly to virtual memory, so the Core memory references above already reflect every access actually served. In configurations with an MMU, a core-side access doesn't necessarily correspond 1:1 to a physical memory access: a TLB hit needs none, and a page-table walk needs several. Physical memory is also doubleword-addressed in this model (see Model Components), a different unit than a core-side access. This is why physical memory accesses are reported separately, only where an MMU is present, rather than folded into the Core table above.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of the peripheral devices modeled here is to include a bare minimum set of devices that make the model realistic, and sufficient to port a basic operating system on top of it.

  • Timer A countdown timer, used for generating periodic interrupts, the kind an OS uses for context switching.
  • Interrupt Controller Routes hardware interrupts to the hardware threads of every core, and lets threads interrupt each other (inter-processor interrupts).
  • Serial Device A single device for I/O.

The register formats, addresses, and behavior documented here are credited to the AJIT processor documentation, Chapter 8, "Basic peripherals available for AJIT systems". The device models in this project are designed to be compatible with it, except for the deviations listed at the end of this page.

docs.title: Connection diagram
docs.text:
A programmer's view of how the devices connect.

There is a single shared set of devices in the system, on the memory side of the MMU. Every device has registers that are read and written over the same physical bus the core uses for main memory, by physical address. In the Sitar model a bridge routes each access to main memory or to the devices (see Model Configurations). Each device also has its own individual signal pins, unrelated to the bus:

  • Timer: a clock_in input, and a timer_int_out output to the Interrupt Controller.
  • Serial Device: serial_in/serial_out pins, and a serial_int_out output to the Interrupt Controller.
  • Interrupt Controller: timer_int_out/serial_int_out inputs, an external interrupt input (env_int_in, reserved for an external source such as an accelerator), and one interrupt_level output per hardware thread. Inter-processor interrupts are generated inside it, from its own IPI registers.

docs.title: Device address map
docs.text:
The addresses match AJIT's default device map, so software written for AJIT finds every device where it expects it. Reach them with the MMU bypass ASI (0x20, see Appendix I of the SPARC V8 manual), or with an ordinary translated access if the page is identity mapped.

Device : Register Address Access type Instruction example Interrupt Controller : Control, thread (core c, thread t) 0xFFFF3000 + 4*(2c+t) word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Interrupt Controller : IPI registers 0xFFFF3080 to 0xFFFF30CB word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Timer : Control 0xFFFF3100 word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Serial : Control 0xFFFF3200 word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Serial : Tx 0xFFFF3204 byte (8-bit) stba %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Serial : Rx 0xFFFF3208 byte (8-bit) lduba [%rd] 0x20, %rs Serial : Baud limit / baud control 0xFFFF320c word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Serial : Baud frequency 0xFFFF3210 word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20

%rd holds the register's address, loaded with set beforehand. C programs can use the AJIT-compatible routines in compiler/include/ instead (see C Programs).

An access to an address in the device window (0xFFFF0000 and up) that no device decodes reads as 0 and ignores writes, with a warning from the simulator.

docs.title: Interrupt levels
docs.text:
Source IRL Priority Timer 10 Highest IPI (inter-processor interrupt) 11 Serial 12 Env (external, e.g. an accelerator) 14 Lowest

For each hardware thread, the Interrupt Controller priority-encodes the active sources that thread's mask enables: the lowest IRL number among them wins. See the Interrupt Controller page for the details.

docs.title: Deviations from the AJIT Processor
docs.text:
Differences from AJIT's own device models (in its multi-core C model, devices/src/ in the ajit-toolchain repository), each small and deliberate:

  • Timer clock. AJIT's timer counts wall-clock time on the host. Here it counts model ticks, one per core cycle by default (a configurable divider). In hardware the timer may run off its own clock, so timer counts are not hardware time.
  • IPI register decode. AJIT decodes the IPI word index from the low 6 address bits only, so its last three IPI words alias onto the first three (the lock word lands on thread 0's message). Here all 19 words are separate.
  • Serial baud registers and UART_reset. Present here (from the AJIT processor description), absent from AJIT's C model. The baud values are stored and read back but do not set the model's transmit timing, which is its own knob.
  • Serial receive disable. Writing Rx_en=0 disables the receiver from any state here, as the AJIT processor description says. AJIT's C model only does so while holding a received byte.
  • Serial transmit disable. Writing Tx_en=0 while a byte is still being transmitted finishes sending it first, so no program output is lost.
  • Unmapped device addresses read as 0 and ignore writes, with a warning, the same as AJIT's bridge does for any unmapped address.

docs.title: Interrupt Controller
docs.text:
A single, shared Interrupt Controller (IRC) routes the system's interrupt sources to the hardware threads of every core. It is AJIT's multi-thread interrupt controller. It has two parts:

  • one slot per hardware thread, each with its own control register, its own state, and its own interrupt_level output to that thread;
  • an inter-processor interrupt (IPI) block, which lets any thread interrupt any other (or itself).

All its registers are accessed with word loads and stores. See Peripheral Devices for the connection diagram and the full address map.

docs.title: Interrupt sources
docs.text:
Source IRL Reaches Timer 10 every slot (each slot's mask decides) IPI 11 the destination slot only Serial Device 12 every slot (each slot's mask decides) External (env_int_in) 14 every slot (each slot's mask decides)

The external input is reserved for a source outside this device set, such as an accelerator. It is not driven by any device here.

docs.title: Slots
docs.text: There are 8 slots, enough for 4 cores with 2 hardware threads each. The slot for core c, thread t is number 2c + t, and its control register is at 0xFFFF3000 + 4*(2c + t). A program finds its own core and thread with rd %asr29, which reads (core << 8) | thread (in C, ajit_get_core_and_thread_id()). The single-core configurations here are core 0, thread 0, so they use slot 0 at 0xFFFF3000.

docs.title: Control register
docs.text:
Bits Field Access Description [0] Enable read/write 1 enables this slot. Writing 0 disables it and drops its interrupt_level. [15:1] Level mask read/write Bit i set: interrupt level i is delivered to this thread. [30:16] Active sources read only Bit 15+i is 1 while a source at level i is active, whether or not it is masked. [31] Interrupting read only 1 while the slot is in IRC_INTERRUPTING.

The mask bit positions equal each source's level, so masking a source is a bitwise AND. Writes to the read-only bits are ignored. The active sources field lets software see a source that is pending but masked, and is readable even while the slot is disabled.

docs.title: Priority
docs.text: When more than one enabled level is active at once, the lowest level number wins: Timer (10) > IPI (11) > Serial (12) > External (14).

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Each slot runs its own state machine:

  • IRC_DISABLED The reset state. interrupt_level is 0. A write that sets the enable bit moves to IRC_ENABLED.
  • IRC_ENABLED Watches the sources. As soon as any level enabled in the mask is active, interrupt_level is set to that level (the highest-priority one, if more than one), and the slot moves to IRC_INTERRUPTING.
  • IRC_INTERRUPTING interrupt_level stays asserted, even if the source goes away, until software clears the enable bit.

A write that clears the enable bit, from any state, immediately drops interrupt_level and moves to IRC_DISABLED. A write that sets the enable bit while already enabled or interrupting only updates the mask.

docs.title: Handling an interrupt
docs.text:
The usual sequence, which AJIT's own bare-metal routines follow (and which compiler/include/ajit_mt_irc.h implements, see C Programs):

  1. The interrupt trap for level L is taken.
  2. The handler disables its own slot, which drops interrupt_level.
  3. It clears the source (for example, disables the timer, or reads the Serial device's Rx register).
  4. It enables its slot again. If another enabled source is still active, the slot delivers it next.

docs.title: Inter-processor interrupts (IPI)
docs.text:
The IPI block is 19 words at 0xFFFF3080:

Offset Register Description 0x00 IPI mask Bit s: IPIs to slot s are enabled. 0x04 IPI value Bit s: an IPI is pending for slot s. 0x08 to 0x47 Messages 8 bytes per destination slot (slot s at 0x08 + 8s), for software. 0x48 Lock A word for software to use as a lock.

Slot s sees an IPI (level 11) while bit s is set in both the mask and the value. To interrupt another thread, a thread writes a message for it, then sets its bit in the value register (and in the mask, if not already set). The interrupted thread reads its message and clears its value bit. Locking around these steps, with the lock word or otherwise, is up to software, exactly as in AJIT. The routines in compiler/include/ajit_ipi.h (__ajit_set_ipi_interrupt__() and friends) do the register work.

docs.title: Serial Device
docs.text:
A memory-mapped serial device (UART) that exchanges bytes between the core and an external I/O device. It has serial_in/serial_out pins, a serial_int_out output pin to the Interrupt Controller (IRL 12), and communicates with the core over the shared address/data bus through its own set of registers. See Peripheral Devices for the connection diagram and the full address map.

A single instance is modeled. A self-tuning variant, which auto-detects baud rate from an initial calibration byte, is not used here.

docs.title: Registers
docs.text:
Register Width Access Control 32-bit word (ld/st) Tx 8-bit byte store (stb), write only Rx 8-bit byte load (ldub), read only Baud limit / baud control 32-bit word Baud frequency 32-bit word

See Peripheral Devices for the address of each register.

Each register has its own address. Tx and Rx are byte registers: a byte store to Tx's address sends that byte, and a byte load from Rx's address returns the received byte.

docs.title: Control register bit-fields
docs.text: Bit Field Description [0] Tx_en Transmit enable. [1] Rx_en Receive enable. [2] Rx_interrupt_enable If set, receiving a byte raises an interrupt. [3] Tx_full (read-only) Set once the CPU writes Tx, cleared once it is transmitted. [4] Rx_full (read-only) Set once a byte is received into Rx, cleared once the CPU reads it. [5] UART_reset Writing 1 resets both state machines to their reset state (a byte still being transmitted is dropped). Always reads 0. Present only in the newest of the AJIT references consulted, see the deviations list on the Peripheral Devices page.

docs.title: Baud rate
docs.text:
The baud-limit and baud-frequency registers are computed from a desired baud rate and clock frequency, from the GCD of 16 times the baud rate and the clock frequency:

gcd            = GCD(16 x baud_rate, clock_frequency)
baud_frequency = (16 x baud_rate) / gcd
baud_limit     = (clock_frequency / gcd) - baud_frequency

The model stores both registers and reads them back, but they do not set its transmit timing. How long a byte takes to transmit is the model's own txTicksPerByte setting (default 1 cycle, see Model Configuration Settings).

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The device is modeled by two independent state machines, transmit and receive, sharing the one control register above.

docs.title: Transmit
docs.text:
• TX_DISABLED The reset state. A write of Tx_en=1 clears Tx_full and moves to TX_ENABLED.
  • TX_ENABLED Waits for a Tx register write. On one, Tx_full is set and the device moves to TX_TRANSMITTING.
  • TX_TRANSMITTING Once the byte finishes transmitting, Tx_full is cleared and the device returns to TX_ENABLED. A Tx write while still transmitting is dropped.

A write of Tx_en=0 from any state returns to TX_DISABLED. If a byte is still being transmitted, it is sent first.

To send a byte: enable the transmitter, write the byte to the Tx register, then poll Tx_full until it clears before writing the next one (or disable the transmitter).

docs.title: Receive
docs.text:
• RX_DISABLED The reset state. A write of Rx_en=1 clears Rx_full and moves to RX_ENABLED.
  • RX_ENABLED Waits for a byte on the serial_in pin. On one, Rx_full is set, an interrupt is raised if Rx_interrupt_enable is set, and the device moves to RX_DATA_RECEIVED.
  • RX_DATA_RECEIVED Once the CPU reads the Rx register, Rx_full and the interrupt are cleared and the device returns to RX_ENABLED.

A write of Rx_en=0 from any state clears Rx_full and the interrupt, and returns to RX_DISABLED. While the receiver is disabled or still holds an unread byte, incoming bytes wait, they are not lost.

The receiver supports two usage modes, selected by Rx_interrupt_enable:

  • Polling mode (Rx_interrupt_enable=0): enable the receiver, poll Rx_full until it sets, then read the Rx register (and disable the receiver, or leave it enabled for the next byte).
  • Interrupt mode (Rx_interrupt_enable=1): enable the receiver, wait for the interrupt, then read the Rx register (and disable the receiver, or leave it enabled for the next byte).

docs.title: Where the bytes go in the simulator
docs.text:
The serial device exists so a program can show output and take input. By default every transmitted byte is written straight to the simulator's own standard output, as the program sends it. Received bytes come from an input file. Every configuration with devices accepts:

Option Effect --serial-in <file> Bytes received on serial_in come from this file, in order. --serial-out <file> Transmitted bytes go to this file instead of standard output. --serial-pty A pseudo-terminal carries both directions. The simulator prints its device name, attach any terminal program to it.

Without --serial-in, a file next to the program's .hex with the same name and the extension .serial_in is used, if it exists. That is how a validation test carries its own input.

docs.title: Timer
docs.text: A simple timer that operates only in one-shot mode. It has a clock_in input pin, a timer_int_out output pin to the Interrupt Controller, and communicates with the core over the shared address/data bus through a single control register, accessed with word load/stores only. See Peripheral Devices for the connection diagram and the full address map.

docs.title: Control register
docs.text:
Bits Field Description [0] Timer_en Enable bit. Writing 1 starts the countdown, writing 0 disables the timer. [31:1] Timer_max_count The number of ticks to count, set on the same write that enables the timer.

A read of the Control register returns it as last written, the same as AJIT. The live count is not readable. Byte stores update only the bytes they select.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Software writes a maximum count into the control register and sets the enable bit in the same write. From that point, the timer counts clock_in edges, starting from 0. When the count reaches the maximum, the timer asserts its interrupt output (IRL 10, see Peripheral Devices) and stops counting. A maximum count of 0 or 1 both fire on the first edge. The interrupt output stays asserted until software explicitly disables the timer.

In the simulator, one clock_in edge is one core cycle by default. A divider makes it every n cycles instead (--timer-tick-divider <n>, or the timerTickDivider setting, see Model Configuration Settings). In hardware the timer may run off a different clock than the core, so timer counts here are model ticks, not hardware time.

  • TIMER_DISABLED The reset state. The interrupt output is 0. A write of Timer_en=1 clears the count, captures Timer_max_count, and moves to TIMER_ENABLED.
  • TIMER_ENABLED Counts up. The interrupt output is 0. When the count reaches Timer_max_count, the interrupt output is asserted, and the timer moves to TIMER_INTERRUPTING. A further write of Timer_en=1 does not restart it.
  • TIMER_INTERRUPTING The timer stops counting. The interrupt output stays asserted until the CPU writes Timer_en=0, which clears it and returns the timer to TIMER_DISABLED.

A write of Timer_en=0 from any state immediately clears the count and the interrupt output, and moves to TIMER_DISABLED.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: A free running 64-bit counter across ASR[31] and ASR[30], running at the processor clock and read-only, is documented separately from this Timer. It is unrelated to it, a CPU-internal cycle counter rather than a memory-mapped, software-configured countdown timer. Our Sitar model does not yet implement this counter.

docs.title: SPARC V8 Architecture
docs.text:
SPARC (Scalable Processor ARChitecture) is a RISC instruction set architecture originally developed at Sun Microsystems, derived from the Berkeley RISC I/II research designs. SPARC V8 is the 32-bit revision of this architecture, standardized as ANSI/IEEE Std 1754-1994. See the Wikipedia SPARC article for general background and history.

SPARC's most distinctive architectural feature is a register window file. A procedure call can get a fresh set of registers without spilling to memory, simply by advancing a circular window into a larger physical register file.

The authoritative specification is The SPARC Architecture Manual, Version 8, included in this repository. This project's model follows it closely, with section references cited throughout the source (model/cpp_common_code/SparcCore.cpp in particular).

docs.title: Why this page exists
docs.text:
The manual PDF has no hyperlinked table of contents or bookmarks of its own, so jumping to a specific chapter or section means scrolling through 295 pages by hand. Every entry in the tables below links directly to that chapter, appendix, or section's own starting page in the bundled PDF.

Page numbers below are the manual's own printed page numbers (the ones in each page's footer, also what this project's own source comments cite), not the PDF file's raw page count. The two drift apart by the end of the document.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Chapter Title What it's about Pages 1 Introduction What SPARC is, its design goals and principal features, and how conformance/compliance is defined. 1-8 2 Overview The architecture end to end, briefly: registers, instruction categories, traps, memory. The best single starting point for a first read. 9-16 3 Data Formats Integer, floating-point (single/double/quad), and tagged-arithmetic data formats. 17-22 4 Registers The register file and windowing mechanism in full detail, PSR/WIM/TBR and every other state register. 23-42 5 Instructions The instruction set itself: formats, addressing modes, every opcode. 43-58 6 Memory Model Total Store Ordering (TSO) and Partial Store Ordering (PSO), and what ordering guarantees software can rely on. 59-68 7 Traps Trap handling, priorities, and the trap table, directly relevant to how every test program in this repository halts. See Writing and Running Assembly Programs. 69-80

docs.text:
The manual skips the letter I (to avoid confusion with the numeral 1), so there is no Appendix I.

The reference to look an opcode up in. 87-150 C ISP Descriptions The same instructions again, but as precise pseudocode (ISP notation). This is what model/cpp_common_code/SparcCore.cpp implements almost line for line, see the table below. 151-188 D Software Considerations Conventions and assumptions a compiler or operating system can rely on, e.g. register-window overflow/underflow handling. 189-204 E Example Integer Multiplication and Division Routines Worked software routines for multiply/divide/remainder, for implementations that don't have them in hardware. 205-226 F Opcodes and Condition Codes Tables of every opcode's bit encoding and every condition code's meaning. Handy as a quick lookup alongside Appendix B. 227-232 G SPARC ABI Software Considerations The calling convention and binary-compatibility rules SPARC application binaries follow. 233-240 H SPARC Reference MMU Architecture A suggested (not mandatory) MMU design. See Model Components. 241-268 J Programming with the Memory Model An intuitive, example-driven companion to Chapter 6's memory model. 269-280 K Formal Specification of the Memory Model The same memory model again, stated formally and precisely. 281-288 L Implementation Characteristics How specific historical SPARC chips actually implemented the architecture, including which instructions they left unimplemented in hardware. 289-296 M Instruction Set Summary A compact, one-line-per-instruction summary table of the entire instruction set. 297-298 N SPARC IEEE 754 Implementation Recommendations How the floating-point unit should handle IEEE 754 details the standard itself leaves open. 299-303

docs.title: Appendix C in detail
docs.text:
Appendix C is the one this project's core implementation (model/cpp_common_code/SparcCore.cpp) cites most, its section numbers appear directly in source comments throughout that file and model/cpp_common_code/SparcStateMachine.cpp.

SparcStateMachine::runOneCycle() implements this loop directly. 156 C.6 Instruction Dispatch The dispatch_instruction macro: how an instruction is routed to integer, FPop, or CPop execution. 159 C.7 Floating-point Execution The complete_fp_execution macro: floating-point trap checks and the Floating-point State Register (FSR). 160 C.8 Traps The execute_trap macro: how the highest-priority pending trap is selected and dispatched. SparcCore::executeTraps() implements this. 161 C.9 Instruction Definitions The ISP pseudocode for every instruction, one by one. This is the definition each SparcCore::execute_*() function follows. 163 C.10 Floating-Point Operate Instructions Notation specific to the multiple-precision floating-point instructions (register-pair/quad alignment). 184

docs.title: Validation Suite
docs.text:
Validating a processor model can mean different things: functional (does each instruction do the right thing), timing or microarchitectural (does it take the right number of cycles, in the right order), or both. This project's suite, in validation/, is purely functional. There are no timing tests here. Both models drive the exact same SparcCore (see Models), so this one suite validates both, and catches a regression in either.

It checks the core's instruction-level behavior against the SPARC V8 manual, in two ways:

  • validation/asm/, hand-written assembly, each test targeting one instruction (or a small family of closely related ones) in isolation.
  • validation/C/, compiled from freestanding C, each test a small self-validating program (a sort, an FFT, a checksum) exercising many instructions together the way a real program would.

It consists of two things: the tests themselves (see "What's in a test" below), and a script, validation/run_tests.py, that runs them all and prints a pass/fail summary (see "The validation script" below).

This page covers how a test is put together, how to run the suite, and how to add a new one. For actually writing a test program (the trap table, the pass-fail convention, structuring a self-validating C test), see Writing and Running Assembly Programs and Writing and Running C Programs.

docs.title: What's in a test
docs.text:
Every test is a matched set of files sharing one name, for example ADD.s, ADD.hex, ADD.objdump, ADD.vprj, and ADD.expected (validation/asm/integer_alu/Arithmetic/Add/). Only two of these are written by hand:

  • <name>.s or <name>.c, the source program.
  • <name>.vprj, its expected final state, in the human-friendly format described below.

The rest are derived automatically, not hand-written (though .hex and .objdump are still committed as build artifacts, see "The validation script" below for why):

  • <name>.hex, the memory image compiled from the source, loadable directly by either model.
  • <name>.objdump, its disassembly plus full symbol table, useful for finding an address to give gdb, see Examining Core State at Runtime Using GDB.
  • <name>.expected, the .vprj's checks rewritten into the plain format the checker executables themselves take as a direct command-line argument, see Getting Started.

In short, .vprj is what you write, once, by hand. .expected is what run_tests.py generates from it, fresh, every time the test runs. It's never edited directly, and doesn't need to be committed to git.

docs.title: The .vprj expected-results format
docs.text:
SOURCES = ADD.s

RESULTS =
g1=0x00000080
o0=0x00000005
o2=0xFFFFFFFB
  • SOURCES names the paired .s/.c file.
  • Each RESULTS line is either a register check (<name>=<hex value>, register mnemonics g1-g7, o0-o7, l0-l7, i0-i7, f0-f31, psr, fpsr, y, wim, tbr, pc, npc, asr0-asr31) or a memory check (m[<hex addr>]=<hex value>, a word-aligned 32-bit read).
  • Either kind of line accepts an optional trailing mask (m[0x148] = 0x00000021 0x00000021 checks only the bits set in the mask. See validation/asm/floating_point/fp_exceptions/accrued_inexact.s for a real example distinguishing individual FSR bits.)
  • asi = ... lines (an AJIT-format leftover) are recognized and ignored. MemCore is a single flat address space with no ASI distinction.

Before running a test, run_tests.py parses this and normalizes it into the plain REG <name> <hex value> [mask] / MEM <addr> <hex value> [mask] format, writing it to a .expected file alongside the test.

Two optional lines, used by the device tests:

  • STARTUP = crt0_interrupts.s, before RESULTS, links that startup file instead of compiler/crt0.s (C tests only).
  • serial_out = "text", among the results, checks the exact bytes the program sent out through the Serial device (C-style escapes such as \n and \x41 work). Only configurations with devices check it.

A test's received serial input, if it needs any, is a file named after the test with the extension .serial_in, next to its .hex.

docs.title: The validation script
docs.text:
A two-phase pipeline, so the existing suite can be run without a cross-compiler installed at all.

# phase 1 (needs the sparc-elf toolchain): assembles/compiles .s or .c
# into .hex, only needed when you add or edit a test's source
validation/build_hex.py validation

# phase 2: runs the already-built .hex against a model
validation/run_tests.py validation

[PASS] validation/asm/misc/save_restore/SAVE.vprj
[PASS] validation/asm/misc/stbar_unimp_nop_sethi/STBAR_UNIMP_NOP_SETHI.vprj

<passed>/<total> tests passed

Since .hex files are committed to git, phase 2 alone is enough to run the existing suite. Phase 1 is only needed after adding or editing a .s/.c source, and also (re)generates that test's .objdump.

You can point run_tests.py at any subset too, not just the validation root:

validation/run_tests.py validation/asm/floating_point
validation/run_tests.py validation/C

It recurses to find .vprj files, so nesting is free.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Does --config NAME Which system_models configuration to run against, default core_only. E.g. --config core_mmu runs against model/system_models/core_mmu/'s own executables instead. --sitar Run against the chosen configuration's Sitar-timed model instead of its plain C++ model (the default). Same CLI, same .vprj format, same PASS/FAIL/OVERALL output either way. See Installation step 3 to build it. --max-cycles N Per-test cycle limit, default 200,000. A test that hasn't halted by then is reported as a failure, rather than hanging forever on a genuine bug. A "cycle" means one complete instruction executed against the plain C++ model, and an actual clock cycle against the Sitar-timed model, see Getting Started. -v Show every check's result, not just failures. 
validation/run_tests.py validation --config core_mmu --sitar -v
validation/run_tests.py validation/asm/control_transfer --max-cycles 50000

validation/clean.sh [folder] removes generated build byproducts (.o, .elf, .expected) without touching .hex/.s/.c/.vprj/.objdump.

docs.title: The test collection
docs.text:
Two sub-suites, side by side under validation/, both using the same .vprj format and the same two-phase pipeline above.

  • asm/ Hand-written assembly tests, each targeting one instruction (or a small family of closely related ones, such as every branch condition) in isolation: integer ALU ops, control transfer (branches, traps, call, jump, rett), loads and stores (including atomic and coprocessor variants), and floating point. Organized into category subfolders: integer_alu/, floating_point/, control_transfer/, data_transfer/, misc/. compiler/assemble.sh builds a test's .s into .hex/.objdump, called automatically by build_hex.py above.

  • C/ Self-validating bare-metal C mini-benchmarks, each compiled program exercising a sequence of C-level operations together (loops, arrays, structs, global variables) the way a real program would, rather than one instruction in isolation. compiler/compile_c.sh builds a test's .c the same way. Every test here follows the same shape: compute something, compare it against a golden value computed once on the host machine and hardcoded right there in the source, and report pass (1) or fail (0) in %o0. Its .vprj then only ever has to check o0=1, instead of re-embedding the golden value a second time. See Writing and Running C Programs for the full convention, and array_sum/array_sum.c for a worked example.

    Test What it computes array_sum Sum of a small int array matrix_mul 3x3 integer matrix multiply fft 4-point integer radix-2 FFT root_finding Integer square root via Newton-Raphson integer_sort Bubble sort gcd Euclidean algorithm fibonacci Iterative Fibonacci prime_sieve Sieve of Eratosthenes checksum Byte-array checksum dot_product Integer vector dot product

Alongside them sits test_simple_ADD/, one more .vprj test, but its main job is as the small worked example used throughout the docs (every configuration's run_simple_test.sh reads the files here directly, and log_viewer/ symlinks to the reference trace produced here, rather than keeping their own copies), see validation/README.md.

docs.title: Adding an asm test
docs.text:
1. Pick an existing category folder under validation/asm/ (integer_alu/, floating_point/, control_transfer/, data_transfer/, misc/), or add a new subfolder for a new, focused group of tests.
  2. Write <name>.s. See Writing and Running Assembly Programs for the full format: the required setup, the trap table, and the pass-fail convention every test shares.
  3. Build and run it directly first, to find the actual final register values, see Assembling to generate a memory image (compiler/assemble.sh <name>.s, then model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only <name>.hex with no expected-results argument, prints the final state).
  4. Write <name>.vprj, naming <name>.s as its SOURCES and listing the register (and, if needed, memory) values from step 3 that you want checked, see the format above.
  5. Run validation/build_hex.py <folder> to (re)generate <name>.hex and <name>.objdump through the suite's own tooling (build_hex.py finds a folder's .vprj files and reads SOURCES to know what to build, so this step needs the .vprj to already exist, from step 4).
  6. Run validation/run_tests.py <folder> to check it passes.

No registration step anywhere else, run_tests.py and build_hex.py both recurse automatically.

docs.title: Adding a C test
docs.text:
1. Add a new folder under validation/C/, one per test.
  2. Write <name>.c, freestanding (no libc, see Writing and Running C Programs), following the same self-validating shape as the existing benchmarks: compute something, compare it against a golden value computed on the host, and report pass (1) or fail (0) in %o0.
  3. Write <name>.vprj, naming <name>.c as its SOURCES. Since the test already computed its own pass/fail, its RESULTS is almost always just o0=1.
  4. Run validation/build_hex.py <folder> to generate <name>.hex and <name>.objdump from it (picking compiler/compile_c.sh automatically, based on the .c extension). As with an asm test, this needs the .vprj to already exist, since build_hex.py reads its SOURCES line to know what to build.
  5. Run validation/run_tests.py <folder> to check it passes.

docs.title: Component validation suites
docs.text:
The suite above is purely functional, and purely for the SPARC core itself: every opcode, exercised in isolation or as part of a larger C program. Alongside it, dedicated test suites validate individual components, each living in its own folder:

  • validation/C/mmu/ The MMU: register access, page-table walks, TLB hit/miss/fill, faults, probe and flush, bypass. See Model Components.
  • validation/C/devices/ The timer, interrupt controller (including interrupt delivery to a real trap handler, priority, masking, and IPIs), and serial device (output, polled and interrupt-driven input). Needs core_mmu_devices. See Peripheral Devices. On the sitar_model these tests need more cycles than the default limit, so run them with --max-cycles 5000000.
  • validation/C/caches/ The L1 caches: write-through, staleness until a flush (they are not coherent), device registers never cached, atomics on a cached line. Needs core_l1cache_mmu_devices. The whole suite above also runs through the caches on that configuration, and with every ordinary access cached if you set SPARC_ALWAYS_CACHEABLE=1 in the environment.

A component's tests only pass on a configuration that actually includes that component, e.g. the MMU suite needs core_mmu or a later configuration that also has an MMU, not core_only. See the README in each config's own folder, or the corresponding validation-suite folder, for which configurations a given component's tests run on.

For example, to run the MMU validation suite on core_mmu, build that configuration first (see Getting Started):

model/system_models/core_mmu/cpp_model/build.sh

then run the suite against it, the same way as any other:

validation/run_tests.py validation/C/mmu

This same suite runs unmodified on any other configuration that also includes an MMU, once one exists, such as core_mmu_devices.

docs.title: Credits: validation suite of the AJIT SPARC V8 processor
docs.text:
Most of validation/asm/'s tests, and the scripts that build and run this suite, are adapted from the AJIT processor project (IIT Bombay), specifically its ajit32 instruction-level verification suite. Many more tests have since been added as part of this project (the quad-precision suite, the validation/C/ benchmarks, and the MMU suite above, none of which exist in AJIT's own tests). Tests adapted directly from AJIT carry their original author credit inline, and are listed as such in validation/asm/README.md and Authors. Tests developed as part of this project are not AJIT-derived.

A handful of specific, well-understood divergences between this model's behavior and AJIT's own reference results are documented, with side-by-side expected-vs-actual data, in docs/compliance/README.md, rather than silently patched or dropped. These are kept separate from the maintained suite (docs/compliance/, not validation/), since they represent understood implementation differences from AJIT's own hardware, not bugs in this model.

docs.title: Writing and Running Assembly Programs
docs.text:
In Getting Started, we discussed how you can view and run an existing program provided in this repository on the C++/Sitar models. A variety of asm and C test programs are present in the validation/ folder. For each program, the test source (.s or .c), the generated memory hex file, and the expected-results file are already included.

This section deals with:

  1. writing your own asm programs,
  2. assembling them to generate a memory image for the simulator,
  3. running them on the simulator, and
  4. the standard format for writing a test for inclusion in this project's validation framework.

This section assumes that you have built the models and the toolchain release. See steps 2 and 5 in Installation.

Let's create a copy of the given simple asm program test_simple_ADD, and modify it, for example, using sub instead of add.

mkdir temp_asm
cd temp_asm
cp ../validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.s test_simple_SUB.s

docs.title: Assembling to generate a memory image (.hex)
docs.text:
The conversion of asm/C programs to a memory image requires a cross-compiler toolchain, consisting of an assembler, utilities such as objdump/readelf, and also a compiler (for compiling C to asm).

If not already done in Installation (step 5), run compiler/install_toolchain.sh to create a release.

The toolchain release lives at compiler/toolchain/. Add it to your PATH variable (on Linux systems) by sourcing compiler/toolchain_env.sh, so that its binaries and libraries can be accessed from any location:

source compiler/toolchain_env.sh

Next, this project provides scripts (compiler/assemble.sh, compiler/compile_c.sh) which are convenience wrappers around these toolchain executables.

To assemble a .s to .hex:

compiler/assemble.sh <file.s>

For example, from temp_asm/:

../compiler/assemble.sh test_simple_SUB.s

This also generates test_simple_SUB.objdump, its disassembly plus full symbol table, useful for finding an address to give gdb, see Examining Core State at Runtime Using GDB. See Cross Compiler for more on what's in the bundled toolchain.

docs.title: Running a test program
docs.text:
Rebuild the models with --logging, then run them on this test. From the repo root:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging temp_asm/test_simple_SUB.hex

This prints the final register state once the program halts, see Getting Started for the full walkthrough, including the Sitar-timed model (which takes the identical CLI) and observing the trace in the log viewer.

docs.title: Creating a test
docs.text:
A test is not just any program that runs on a model, but one that gives a pass/fail indication after checking something. In this project, a test consists of a source file and an expected-results file in a specific format, see "Recommended format for a test program" below for how the source file itself needs to be structured to make this possible.

The simulator executables take the following arguments:

sparc_sim_cpp_core_only <hex_file> [expected_results_file] [max_cycles]
  • A hex file (required): the memory image to run.
  • An expected-results file (optional): if given, once the program halts, the final state is checked against it, and the executable prints a PASS/FAIL verdict per check plus an OVERALL result, instead of the detailed state.
  • A cycle limit (optional): caps how long the simulator runs before giving up.

When no expected-results file is passed, as above, the executable just prints the final register state. When one is passed, it's checked directly instead.

Let's write an expected-results file for our test, and run with that. o0 = 5 - 7 = 0xfffffffe, so temp_asm/test_simple_SUB.expected:

REG o0 0xfffffffe

Then run it:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging \
    temp_asm/test_simple_SUB.hex temp_asm/test_simple_SUB.expected

docs.title: Format for the expected-results file
docs.text:
test_simple_SUB.expected is a plain text file, one check per line:

  • REG <name> <hex value> [mask] checks a register (mnemonics g1-g7, o0-o7, l0-l7, i0-i7, f0-f31, psr, fpsr, y, wim, tbr, pc, npc, asr0-asr31).
  • MEM <hex addr> <hex value> [mask] checks a word-aligned 32-bit memory read.

Either kind accepts an optional trailing mask, to check only specific bits.

docs.title: Recommended format for a test program
docs.text:
Because this model does not yet have any operating system, the test program has to be self-sufficient. This means initializing the processor state, setting up a trap table, then running the test part and exiting while indicating pass/fail in some way to the simulator. In the current scheme, the latter is achieved using %g1 as a sentinel register together with a deliberate final trap (ta 0), described in full under "The pass-fail convention" below.

The following shows a typical structure of a test program:

.global main
main:
_start:
    ! 1. Enable traps: PSR ET=1, PS=1, S=1
    mov 0xE0, %l0
    wr %l0, %psr
    nop
    nop
    nop

    ! 2. Point TBR at this file's own trap table
    set trap_table_base, %l0
    wr %l0, 0x0, %tbr
    nop
    nop
    nop

    ! 3. Sentinel: overwritten by the trap number if anything unexpected traps
    mov 0xBAD, %g1

    !======================================
    ! 4. The instruction(s) under test go here
    add %o0, %o1, %o2
    !======================================

    ta 0            ! 5. normal exit
    nop
    nop

not_reached:
    set 0xDEAD, %g1 ! control should never reach here
    ta 0
    nop
    nop

    .align 4096     ! TBR only captures bits 31:12, so the trap table
                     ! must start on a 4096-byte boundary
trap_table_base:
    ! 256 four-instruction slots, one per trap type (0x00-0xff):
    !   mov <trap number>, %g1 ; restore ; ta 0 ; nop
    ! ... (copy this verbatim from any existing test, see below)

Our own test_simple_SUB skips the trap table by simply disabling traps entirely (wr %g0, %psr), the simplest thing that works when nothing in the test could ever trap. Use the fuller structure above instead for anything meant to join validation/asm/, where an unexpected trap needs to be caught rather than silently forcing error_mode for the wrong reason.

Copy the trap table, don't retype it

The 256-entry trap table is always the same boilerplate. Copy it verbatim from any existing test under validation/asm/, then edit only the one slot you actually care about, see "The trap table" below.

docs.title: The pass-fail convention
docs.text:
Every test always halts the same way: a ta 0 taken with traps disabled (ET=0, cleared automatically on trap entry) forces the processor into error_mode per the manual (Appendix C, Section C.8). This is what PROCESSOR STATE: ERROR in sparc_sim_cpp's output means, and it's expected, not a bug.

%g1 distinguishes a clean run from an unexpected trap:

  • If the test's own final ta 0 (step 5 above) is what triggers this, its trap-table slot (SW_trap_0x80) sets %g1 = 0x80. This is success: nothing unexpected happened.
  • If any other trap occurs first (a bug, a mistake in the test, or a trap you're deliberately testing for), it's caught by that trap's own table slot, which records the trap number into %g1 before re-trapping the same way. So %g1's final value tells you exactly what happened, whether the test passed or not.

docs.title: The trap table
docs.text: Each slot is a fixed 4 instructions: mov <tt>, %g1; restore; ta 0; nop. To make a test verify a specific trap actually fires (rather than just detecting an unexpected one), replace that one slot with custom code. For example, validation/asm/floating_point/fp_exceptions/overflow.s replaces its HW_trap_0x08 slot with inc %g2; rett %r18; nop; nop, which increments a counter and resumes execution right after the trapping instruction (via rett), instead of halting. This lets the test both confirm the trap fired (%g2) and continue on to a normal exit (%g1 = 0x80).

docs.title: Adding it to the validation suite
docs.text:
Hand-writing a .expected file and running it yourself works for one test at a time. To run your test alongside the rest of the suite automatically instead, and have it re-checked every time the model changes, the recommended practice is to wrap it as a .vprj file for use with the validation script. See Validation Suite: Adding an asm test for details.

See validation/asm/README.md for the AJIT-adaptation attribution and docs/compliance/README.md for documented, specific divergences from AJIT's own reference results (kept separate from the maintained suite since they represent understood implementation differences, not bugs).

docs.title: Writing and Running C Programs
docs.text: Hand-assembling an algorithm like a sort or an FFT one instruction at a time, the way validation/asm/'s tests do, is tedious once the program is more than a handful of instructions long (see Validation Suite). validation/C/ takes the other approach: write the test as ordinary, freestanding C, compile it with the bundled cross-toolchain, and run it the same way. This page covers writing one, building and running it, and checking its result.

docs.title: No standard library, by design
docs.text:
This model has no operating system. There is nothing for a C standard library to call into. printf has no console to write to. malloc has no OS to request pages from. C programs for this model must be freestanding: no #include <stdio.h>, no libc at all, just the C language itself plus whatever you implement by hand against the flat memory space MemCore provides.

In the configurations with devices (core_mmu_devices and up), the Serial Device is the console: a program writes characters to it, and the simulator prints them. See Using the peripheral devices below.

docs.title: Structuring a test program
docs.text:
Write an ordinary, freestanding C main(). Every test in validation/C/ follows the same self-validating shape: compute something, compare it against a golden value computed once on the host machine and hardcoded right there in the source, and report pass(1)/ fail(0) in %o0. Here's a real one in full, validation/C/array_sum/array_sum.c, summing a small array:

// array_sum.c
//
// A first bare-metal C validation test, and the template every other
// validation/C/ test follows: sums the elements of a small integer array
// in a loop, then checks the result against a golden value computed once
// on the host machine (here, by hand: 1+2+3+4+5=15) and hardcoded below.
// Self-validating this way means the .vprj only ever has to check one
// thing -- that %o0 is 1 -- rather than re-embedding (and risking a
// second, independent typo in) the actual expected sum.
//
// See docs/writing_and_running_c_programs.md and compiler/crt0.s for how
// this gets a working stack, trap table, and pass/fail halt convention,
// the same way every validation/asm/ test does.

int main(void)
{
    int values[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    int sum = 0;
    int i;
    int expected;
    int pass;

    for (i = 0; i < 5; i++)
        sum += values[i];

    expected = 15; // 1+2+3+4+5, computed on the host
    pass = (sum == expected) ? 1 : 0;

    // Report pass(1)/fail(0) in %o0 -- see the file comment above.
    __asm__ volatile ("mov %0, %%o0" : : "r" (pass));

    // Halt: traps are enabled (crt0.s), so this ta 0 is caught by its
    // trap-table slot, which re-traps with traps now disabled, forcing
    // the model into error_mode. That's this project's pass/fail halt
    // convention, see writing_and_running_assembly_programs.md.
    __asm__ volatile ("ta 0");

    // Never reached: ta 0 above always halts the simulation first. This
    // just satisfies the compiler, which otherwise warns that a
    // non-void main() falls off the end without returning a value.
    while (1) {}
    return 0;
}

main() must never return, since there's nothing to return into. The way to end a test is the same mechanism validation/asm/ tests use, described in full in Writing and Running Assembly Programs: a single line of inline assembly, __asm__ volatile ("ta 0"), at the end of main().

Unlike an assembly test, you don't write any of the surrounding setup by hand. compiler/crt0.s is linked ahead of your compiled .c file (entry point overridden to crt0.s's own _start) and does it for you:

  • enables traps and installs the same 256-entry trap table every validation/asm/ test installs,
  • sets up a working stack (needed for any C function using a local variable, which %sp starting at 0 does not provide on its own),
  • initializes %g1 as the pass/fail sentinel,
  • then calls your main().

Here's what that looks like once linked, array_sum's actual entry point, before main even runs:

00000000 <_start>:
       0:   01 00 00 00     nop
       4:   01 00 00 00     nop
       8:   a0 10 20 e0     mov  0xe0, %l0  ! e0 <not_reached+0x98>
       c:   81 8c 00 00     mov  %l0, %psr
      10:   01 00 00 00     nop
      14:   01 00 00 00     nop
      18:   01 00 00 00     nop
      1c:   21 00 00 04     sethi  %hi(0x1000), %l0
      20:   a0 14 20 00     mov  %l0, %l0   ! 1000 <HW_trap_0x00>
      24:   81 9c 20 00     mov  %l0, %tbr
      28:   01 00 00 00     nop
      2c:   01 00 00 00     nop
      30:   01 00 00 00     nop
      34:   1d 03 ff ff     sethi  %hi(0xffffc00), %sp
      38:   9c 13 a3 f0     or  %sp, 0x3f0, %sp ! ffffff0 <memcpy+0xfffdf48>
      3c:   82 10 2b ad     mov  0xbad, %g1
      40:   40 00 07 f0     call  2000 <main>
      44:   01 00 00 00     nop

Matching it up against the four steps above: the mov 0xe0,%l0/wr %l0,%psr pair enables traps (see Writing and Running Assembly Programs for the 0xE0 encoding), sethi/wr ...,%tbr points TBR at the trap table linked in right after it (HW_trap_0x00 onward, the annotation on that line), sethi/or ...,%sp sets up the stack, mov 0xbad,%g1 is the sentinel, and the final call main (with its delay-slot nop) is the handoff into your code. See crt0.s itself for the full explanation of each step.

The result is that a C test's ta 0 halts exactly the same way an assembly test's does, and an unexpected trap during your test is caught the same way too.

Checking the result is then a single line. Its .vprj only ever has to check that %o0 is 1:

SOURCES = array_sum.c

RESULTS =
o0=1

The alternative: checking memory directly

Writing a raw computed value to a global and checking it directly via a .vprj MEM line (the address found in the .objdump's symbol table, or readelf -s array_sum.elf directly) still works. It's the same REG/MEM format validation/asm/ uses, but means the golden value is embedded in two places (the .vprj and, since the test already computes its own pass/fail, the source) instead of one. Doing the comparison in C and reporting a single pass/fail flag avoids that, and doubles as a self-contained mini-benchmark that also happens to check itself. See the rest of validation/C/ for more worked examples.

docs.title: Building and running it
docs.text:
A minimal, freestanding C compiler (GCC 4.4.3) is bundled alongside the existing sparc-elf assembler, linker, readelf, and objdump, installed together by Installation step 5, if you haven't already. See Cross Compiler for what's bundled and why, and for building your own, more modern cross-toolchain instead.

compiler/compile_c.sh your_program.c

This produces your_program.hex, the same kind of memory image compiler/assemble.sh produces for assembly tests, loadable the same way. It also produces your_program.objdump: a readable disassembly of the linked program (useful for seeing what the compiler actually generated, unlike a hand-written .s file, this isn't something you wrote directly), followed by the full symbol table, function and global-variable addresses included. See Examining Core State at Runtime Using GDB.

Run it directly against the model the same way as an assembly test, see Running a test program:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only your_program.hex

docs.title: Using the peripheral devices
docs.text:
compiler/include/ holds header-only routines for the devices, with the same file names, function names, and signatures as AJIT's own bare-metal access routines, so code written for AJIT compiles here unchanged. compile_c.sh puts that folder on the include path.

Header Provides device_addresses.h Every device register address (ADDR_TIMER_CONTROL_REGISTER, ...) and interrupt level (TIMER_IRL, ...). ajit_access_routines.h Physical (MMU-bypass) loads and stores, ajit_get_core_and_thread_id(), and the Timer and Serial routines, e.g. __ajit_serial_putchar_via_bypass__(), __ajit_serial_getchar_via_bypass__(), __ajit_write_timer_control_register_via_bypass__(). ajit_mt_irc.h Interrupt Controller routines (enableInterruptController(), writeInterruptControlRegister(), ...) and interrupt dispatch (ajit_set_interrupt_handler()). ajit_ipi.h Inter-processor interrupts (__ajit_set_ipi_interrupt__(), ...). stdint.h uint32_t and friends, which the bundled compiler does not provide on its own.

Printing a message:

#include "ajit_access_routines.h"

int main(void)
{
    char message[] = "Hello from SPARC\n";
    __ajit_serial_configure_via_bypass__(1, 0, 0);   //enable the transmitter
    __ajit_serial_puts_via_bypass__(message, sizeof(message) - 1);
    __asm__ volatile ("ta 0");
    while (1) {}
}

docs.title: Taking interrupts
docs.text:
The default startup code, crt0.s, halts on every trap other than the final ta 0. A program that takes interrupts links compiler/crt0_interrupts.s instead, which also handles register window overflow and underflow, and sends every interrupt to ajit_generic_interrupt_handler() (in ajit_mt_irc.h). That function calls the handler registered for the interrupt's level:

#include "ajit_access_routines.h"
#include "ajit_mt_irc.h"

volatile int ticks = 0;

void timer_handler(void)
{
    ticks++;
    __ajit_write_timer_control_register_via_bypass__(0);   //clear the source
}

int main(void)
{
    ajit_initialize_interrupt_handlers_to_null();
    ajit_set_interrupt_handler(TIMER_IRL, timer_handler);
    writeInterruptControlRegister(0, 0, (1 << TIMER_IRL) | 1);   //slot 0: enable, timer level
    __ajit_write_timer_control_register_via_bypass__((1000 << 1) | 1);
    while (ticks == 0) {}
    __asm__ volatile ("ta 0");
    while (1) {}
}

Select the interrupt startup code with a STARTUP line in the test's .vprj (see below), or with CRT0=crt0_interrupts.s compile_c.sh ... on the command line. Handlers run with traps enabled but every maskable interrupt masked, so they do not nest.

docs.title: Adding it to the validation suite
docs.text: Same two-phase pipeline as validation/asm/, see Validation Suite. build_hex.py picks compiler/assemble.sh or compiler/compile_c.sh automatically, based on whether a test's SOURCES line names a .s or a .c file. See Validation Suite: Adding a C test for the exact steps.

docs.title: The APARA Engine
docs.text:
APARA is a compute engine designed to sit next to a SPARC (AJIT) processor as an accelerator: a four-threaded VLIW engine with its own instruction and data memories, built for small-integer and low-precision float vector work (dot products, reductions, element-wise arithmetic on 4- to 64-bit elements). The processor loads its programs, starts its threads and moves data in and out of it. The engine was designed at IIT Bombay (Prof. Madhav Desai); this project models it from its documents and its reference model.

The engine's main traits, which these pages explain:

  • Bundles. Up to 8 instructions run in parallel each step, in a thread's program order.
  • Four hardware threads, each with 32 64-bit registers, sharing one five-stage pipeline: when one thread waits, the others keep it busy.
  • Types in every instruction. One register is a 64-bit integer, or 8 $i8 elements, or 16 $f4 floats, chosen by each instruction.
  • Local memories: 16 KB of instructions and 64 KB of data in two banks.

docs.title: In this project
docs.text:
Configuration What it is Status apara one engine on its own; programs and data placed in its memories before the run functional and timing models, tests, tools sparc_apara a SPARC core (with L1 caches, MMU and peripheral devices) and one engine: the SPARC loads and runs the engine's programs, and the engine's DMA and its own loads and stores reach the system's memory functional and timing models, C routines, tests

The pages:

  • Instruction Set: state, types, bundles, every instruction, encodings.
  • Assembly Language and Tools: mcode, our assembler and disassembler, the file formats.
  • Writing and Running Programs: the simulators, the tests.
  • Timing Model: the pipeline and its timing rules.
  • The Engine in a System: sparc_apara, the control and DMA units, the SPARC-side routines.
  • Deviations and Findings: where the model differs from the reference model, and the open questions.

docs.title: The code
docs.text: Where What model/cpp_common_code/apara/ the engine in plain C++: AparaCore (state and execution), AparaInstruction (decoding), AparaOperations (the arithmetic), AparaTypes (number formats), AparaFiles and AparaRun (files and simulator runs), AparaTiming (latency table, BTB, pipeline tokens) model/sitar_component_models/Apara*.sitar the pipeline: AparaEngine and its five stage modules model/system_models/apara/ the configuration: cpp_model/ (apara_sim_cpp) and sitar_model/ (apara_sim_sitar) model/cpp_common_code/apara/ (system) AparaControlCore (CCU), AparaDmaCore (DMA), AparaSystemCore (all three, for the cpp model) model/sitar_component_models/AparaHost.sitar, SystemInterconnect.sitar the engine's host side and the two-master bus, in Sitar model/system_models/sparc_apara/ the configuration compiler/include/apara_access_routines.h, compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py SPARC-side routines; an engine program as a C array validation/C/apara/ the SPARC-side tests compiler/apara/ the assembler, disassembler, their library mcode.py, vim syntax validation/apara/ the tests and their runner

docs.title: APARA Assembly Language and Tools
docs.text: APARA programs are written in mcode, the engine's assembly language, and assembled with our own tools in compiler/apara/ (Python 3, standard library only). For any program the APARA reference assembler accepts, the tools write the same object file, word for word: they were checked on every valid program in the APARA repository's test and verification folders.

docs.title: A first program
docs.text:
// Sum the 8-bit elements of a vector, store the result.
//@ reg: 0 $r1 0x0102030405060708

sum:
    ||
        $vreduce + $r2 ($vi8) $r1       // 1+2+...+8 = 36
    ;
store:
    ||
        $st ($i64) [$r0 + 16] $r2       // DMEM bytes 16..23
    ;
    || $halt ;

A program is a sequence of bundles, each ||, one to eight instructions, ;. A bundle may have a label (sum:). // starts a comment. Lines starting //@ are directions for the test runner (Ref Writing and Running Programs); the assembler ignores them. Every instruction is listed in APARA Instruction Set.

docs.title: What the assembler does
docs.text:
1. Parses and checks every instruction: register numbers, types, immediate and increment ranges, the operations each type allows (Ref the error messages below).
  2. Checks each bundle: at most 8 instructions, one branch/call/return, 4 loads/stores, one divide or square root, and no register written by two instructions.
  3. Closes each bundle with $nulls up to its capacity: 8 if it holds a control transfer, load/store, divide or square root, else the next power of two.
  4. Places the bundles, each at a multiple of its size, filling gaps with $null pad bundles of 4, 2 and 1 slots.
  5. Arranges the lanes of each 8-slot bundle: the control transfer in lane 0, a divide or square root in lane 1, loads and stores in lanes 4 to 7, the other instructions in source order in the free lanes.
  6. Resolves labels: a branch or call holds its target relative to its own address (its bundle's address plus its lane).
  7. Encodes, setting bit 31 on each bundle's first word.

These are the reference tools' passes (mcode_align then mcode_assemble) in one step.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py prog.mcode                 # writes prog.obj
python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py prog.mcode -o out.obj \
        --aligned prog.aligned.mcode --listing prog.lst
python3 compiler/apara/apara_dis.py prog.obj                  # mcode to standard output
  • --aligned writes the program as placed and arranged, every bundle with its address: the program the engine actually runs.
  • --listing writes each word's address, encoding and instruction.
  • apara_dis.py turns an object file back into mcode, with labels L_<address> for branch and call targets. Its output assembles back to the same object file.

An error stops the assembly:

prog.mcode:12: error: $r2 is written twice in this bundle (also at line 11)

Some messages and what they mean:

Message Cause immediate 600 is out of range (-512 to 511) immediates are 10-bit signed a bundle holds at most one divide or square root the engine has one shared divider floats have only + - * / no logic or shifts on float types the registers from $r30 run past $r31 a $u256 transfer needs 4 consecutive registers a vector cast changes the element width by one step ($vi8) to ($vi32) needs two casts undefined label x (the reference assembler silently uses 0)

python3 compiler/apara/test_mcode.py runs the tools' own unit tests.

docs.title: File formats
docs.text:
The formats of the reference tools, so files move freely between the two tool sets. Numbers are hexadecimal; ! starts a comment.

File Lines Example object (.obj) <word index>: <instruction word> 8: 80000000 data (data.map) <dword index>: <64-bit value> 10: 0x0102030405060708 registers <thread> <register> <value> 0 1f 0x10 results <thread> pc <pc> [mask] 0 pc 0x21 <thread> reg <register> <value> [mask] 0 reg 0x5 0x67 <thread> mem <dword index> <value> [mask] 0 mem 0x4 0x00aa000000001234 <thread> error <ERROR> [mask] (ours) 0 error 0x2000000

A mask, if given, selects the bits compared. A data file's dword index is taken modulo the DMEM size: index 0x10 is DMEM bytes 0x80 to 0x87.

docs.title: Editor support
docs.text:

docs.title: APARA: Deviations and Findings
docs.text:
The model is our own implementation of the APARA engine. Its sources, in order of authority for us: the microarchitecture document (timing and structure), the ISA document (engine_isp/isa/isa.txt), and the reference model McodeMachine with its tools (mcode_align, mcode_assemble, mcode_run). For every program the reference tools handle correctly the model gives the same results: the same object file from the assembler, and the same final state (PC, registers, DMEM) from a run, checked on every valid program of the APARA repository and on our own tests (Ref Writing and Running Programs).

This page lists where the model differs from the reference model, why, and the open questions in the sources, for review with the APARA's designer. Tests that depend on a deviation are marked //@ deviation in validation/apara/tests/ (dev_*.mcode).

docs.title: Semantics

the 2-bit increment is not sign-extended (--1 adds 3) $rs2 written only with an increment, as $rs2 + increment, signed an ($i8) test clobbered a 64-bit $rs2 6 an unsigned test (branch, $cmov) compares as a signed 64-bit value; a float test compares the sign-extended bit pattern unsigned compares unsigned; floats compare by value, NaN satisfies only != ($u64) 2^63 > 0 was false 7 a float $dot $accumulate ignores the accumulator starts from $rd's f32 value the instruction's meaning 8 no $fsqrt (an error, result 0) implemented for f32 and f64 (as pow(x, 0.5), as the reference's helpers would) isa.txt 9 no float casts (an error) implemented: integer to float converts the full source value; float to integer truncates toward zero and saturates; NaN gives 0 isa.txt lists them 10 a scalar integer cast from a 64-bit source is not truncated to the destination width (narrower sources are) always truncated consistency 11 no float divide for f4, f8, f16 (assert) every float width divides 12 a load/store's negative increment is added as an unsigned 32-bit value (bytes * increment is evaluated as unsigned): --1 on an 8-byte load adds 0xFFFFFFF8 a signed 64-bit add a C++ promotion bug 13 float ALU operations other than + - * /, and vector ones other than + - *, assert illegal instruction (the assembler rejects them) 14 the branch decoder reads rs2 as 6 bits [5:0], including the offset's low bit bits [4:0] an odd offset selected a register 32 higher
