docs.title: The engine in a system (sparc_apara)
docs.text:
From the hardware's Aa sources (cpu/ccu/ccu.aa, dma/control.aa, data_mem/*.aa), which the reference model does not cover:

# Source This model Why 26 dma/control.aa uses control-word bit 3 as interrupt enable, as the error flag on completion, and (written) to clear the interrupt; a command with it set never starts flags [0] scheduled, [1] started, [2] completed, [3] interrupt enable, [4] error one meaning per bit 27 CCU.TXT calls command 7 "wait-on-complete"; ccu.aa polls (non-blocking), so its interrupt fires only if a poll finds the thread already stopped without interrupt enable, a poll; with it, the command waits for the stop, then interrupts an interrupt a program can wait for 28 command 8 (step) executes the instruction in R2 at PC R1 one bundle from IMEM at R1, with local data only; R7 := the next PC debugging use 29 command 9 returns the RAS's 52-bit internal state R6 := depth, R7 := top 30 (reset leaves registers to the hardware's reset) reset keeps the registers, clears PC, RAS and ERROR registers set before a run survive a reset

The rule for local addresses follows the hardware (isInEngineDataMem): in a system only the engine's own DMEM window is local. The reference model aliases every address into DMEM; the standalone apara configuration keeps that behavior.

docs.title: Open questions in the sources
docs.text:
Carried by the model as explicit, documented choices (D1-D7 from the first review of the sources, then the findings since):

  • D1, opcode numbering from 0x16. The Aa_model's parameters.aa and OperatorClassification.txt disagree. The model uses the assembler's numbering (isa/parameters.aa) and keys its latencies by instruction class, not opcode.
  • D2, memory operations per bundle. The microarch doc says at most two (one per DMEM port); the slot rules, mcode_align and the reference documentation allow four. The model allows four, two ports, same-bank accesses one after another.
  • D3, slot rules. The model enforces the microarch doc's (and the assembler produces them).
  • D4, EXEC's structure. "Holds one bundle until the slowest finishes" versus "internally pipelined, full rate". The model is pipelined, results in order; engine.exec.pipelined = false gives the other.
  • D5, latencies. DIV and FSQRT 10 cycles (verbal), VREDUCE 2 and CMOV 1 (assumed): not in OperatorClassification.txt.
  • D6, the parameter template. Its comments and values disagree on the DMEM and configuration base addresses; the model follows the values (they agree with the AFB demultiplexer's decode).
  • D7, a push into a full RAS. Halts the thread (microarch doc) versus "blocks the engine" (ISA text): the model halts the thread.
  • Same-bank order. The microarch doc serializes same-bank accesses in slot order; the Aa_model does not fix an order. The model uses slot order.
  • Exception code 4, "integer square root of a negative number", is in the hardware's exception table, but isa.txt says there is no integer square root. The model has none (the code is unused).
  • The BTB is shared by the four threads; two threads' branches that alias to one entry evict each other. Modeled as described.
  • REGFILE and WRITEBACK. The microarch doc's channel table shows lock releases going from WRITEBACK to REGFILE, its text (from the Aa_model) has REGFILE reading EXEC's results and forwarding them to the retire daemon. The model follows the text; with two tokens it is the version that sustains one bundle per cycle.

docs.title: APARA Instruction Set
docs.text: This page is the programmer's reference for the APARA engine as this model implements it: its state, its data types, bundles, and every instruction. The model follows the APARA ISA (engine_isp/isa/isa.txt in the APARA repository) and the reference model, McodeMachine; where the two disagree, or the reference model has a defect, the model's choice is listed in Deviations and Findings.

docs.title: Engine state
docs.text:
An engine runs up to four threads. They share the engine's two local memories and its execution pipeline, and each has its own architectural state:

State Size Notes PC 32 bits a word index into IMEM, not a byte address $r0 .. $r31 64 bits each $r0 reads as 0; writes to it are dropped return-address stack (RAS) 64 entries pushed by $call, popped by $return ERROR 32 bits why the thread stopped (below) Memory Size Organization IMEM 16 KB, 4096 instruction words read by the pipeline 8 words (one line) at a time DMEM 64 KB, 8192 64-bit words two 32 KB banks (address bit 15), big-endian

DMEM addresses are byte addresses. Each 64-bit word ("dword") is big-endian: the byte at an address with (address & 7) == 0 is bits [63:56]. In the standalone engine every data address aliases into DMEM (modulo 64 KB). In a system (the sparc_apara configuration), other addresses reach system memory.

A thread is inactive until started, then running until it executes $halt or meets an exception, after which it is halted. ERROR tells which:

ERROR bits Meaning 26 return-address stack error: $call with the RAS full, or $return with it empty 25 the thread executed $halt 24 an exception stopped the thread [23:0] one 3-bit exception code per bundle slot, slot s in bits [3s+2 : 3s] Code Exception 1 integer divide by zero 2 float divide by zero 3 a float arithmetic result is not a number (NaN) 4 (reserved: integer square root of a negative number in the hardware's table; there is no integer square root) 5 float square root of a negative number 6 memory address not a multiple of the transfer size 7 illegal instruction, an instruction in a slot it cannot use, or no valid bundle at the PC (slot 0)

A bundle that raises an exception changes nothing: no register, memory or PC update happens, and the thread halts with its PC at that bundle.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
Every instruction that operates on data names a type, written in parentheses: ($i32), ($vf16). A type is an element width and three flags.

Types Meaning $i4 $i8 $i16 $i32 $i64 signed integers $u4 $u8 $u16 $u32 $u64 unsigned integers $u128 $u256 2 and 4 registers, for memory transfers only $f4 $f8 $f16 $f32 $f64 floats $vi4 .. $vi32, $vu4 .. $vu32, $vf4 .. $vf32 vectors of signed, unsigned or float elements

Scalars narrower than 64 bits live in the low bits of a register. A signed operation sign-extends its operands from the type's width; an unsigned integer operation uses the full 64-bit register values. Integer ALU results are 64 bits. Float results are in the type's format, in the low bits.

Vectors pack 64/width elements in one register, element 0 in the most significant bits: $r1 = 0x0102030405060708 as ($vi8) holds the elements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 in that order.

Floats: f32 and f64 are IEEE single and double precision. f16 is IEEE half precision (E5M10, bias 15), f8 is E4M3 (bias 7), and f4 holds the values ±{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, ∞, NaN}. Arithmetic on narrow floats is done in double precision and rounded back with one round bit (round half up on the magnitude), saturating to infinity, flushing to zero below the smallest subnormal: the reference model's conversion rules exactly.

docs.title: Bundles
docs.text:
Instructions are 32 bits. They run in bundles of 1, 2, 4 or 8, all the instructions of a bundle in parallel:

  • Every instruction of a bundle reads the registers as they were before the bundle. A bundle that swaps two registers just copies each into the other.
  • Memory accesses happen in slot order: a load sees a store of an earlier slot of the same bundle.
  • Register writes apply in slot order, but no two instructions of a bundle may write the same register (the assembler checks this).

A bundle that holds a branch, call, return, load, store, divide or square root must have 8 slots; any other bundle has the next power of two (1, 2, 4 or 8) at least as large as its instruction count. Unused slots hold $null. A bundle's address is a multiple of its size. In an 8-slot bundle, a branch/call/return must be in slot 0, a divide or square root in slot 1, and loads and stores in slots 4 to 7. The assembler does all of this (closing, padding, placing, arranging); the engine checks it.

Bit 31 of an instruction word is set on the first instruction of each bundle; bits [30:26] are the opcode.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: Syntax in the forms the assembler accepts. $rd is the destination, $rs1/$rs2 the sources, imm a signed 10-bit immediate (-512 to 511).

docs.title: Arithmetic and logic (scalar)
docs.text:
+  $rd (type) $rs1 $rs2       // also: - * / | & ^ ~| ~& ~^ << >>
+  $rd (type) $rs1 imm

$rd = $rs1 op $rs2 (or imm). ~|, ~&, ~^ are NOR, NAND, XNOR. For integer types, every operation; a signed >> is arithmetic, shift counts use their low 6 bits, and / truncates toward zero (divide by zero is exception 1). For float types, only + - * / (divide by zero is exception 2, a NaN result exception 3).

docs.title: Vector arithmetic
docs.text:
$v + $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2                // also: - *
$v + $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2 $replicate     // $rs2's low element for every element

Element by element, results wrapping at the element width.

docs.title: Dot product and reduction
docs.text:
$dot $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2                // sum of element products
$dot $accumulate $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2    // ... plus $rd
$vreduce + $rd (vtype) $rs1               // also: * | & ^ ~^

Integer dot products and reductions give a 64-bit result; float ones an f32, accumulated in single precision one element at a time.

docs.title: Square root
docs.text: $fsqrt $rd ($f32) $rs1                    // or ($f64)

docs.title: Casts
docs.text:
$cast (dtype) $rd (stype) $rs2

Scalar to scalar, or vector to vector. A scalar cast converts the low bits of $rs2: integers are sign- or zero-extended by the source type, then truncated to the destination width; integer/float conversions convert the value (float to integer truncates toward zero and saturates; NaN gives 0). A vector cast converts every element and may change the element width by one step: widening writes $rd and $rd+1, narrowing reads $rs2 and $rs2+1.

docs.title: Moving and arranging bits
docs.text:
$set   $rd index value          // $rd = value << (8*index), value 16 bits, index 0-7
$slice $rd high low $rs2        // $rd = bits [high:low] of $rs2
$pack  P $rd W $rs2             // the low W bits of $rs2, $rs2+1, ... packed into P bits
$cmov  (type) $rs1 cond [incr] $rd $rs2   // if $rs2 cond 0 then $rd = $rs1

$pack 64 $r8 16 $r2 builds $r8 from the low 16 bits of $r2 .. $r5, $r2 in the most significant position; P above 64 writes P/64 registers. $cmov tests its last register ($rs2), and an optional increment (++1, --1, --2) is added to $rs2 after the test. value may be decimal or hexadecimal written _h1234.

Conditions, for $cmov and branches, compare a value with 0: `== > <

= <= !=. Signed integers compare as values of the type's width, unsigned integers as 64-bit unsigned values, floats by value (a NaN satisfies only!=`).

docs.title: Loads and stores
docs.text:
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + $rs2]        $st (type) [$rs1 + $rs2] $rd
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + $rs2 ++n]    // then $rs2 += n * transfer size (n: -16..15)
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + imm]

The address is $rs1 + $rs2 (or + imm), and must be a multiple of the transfer size (exception 6). 1-, 2-, 4- and 8-byte transfers move one register (signed loads sign-extend); $u128 and $u256 move 2 and 4 registers, $rd up. A vector type moves one element.

docs.title: Control transfer
docs.text:
? (type) $rs2 cond [incr] $goto label   // branch if $rs2 cond 0; then $rs2 += incr
$call label                             // or $call $rs2: target = this address + $rs2
$return
$halt
$null

Branch and call targets are relative to the instruction's own address. $call pushes the address of the next bundle on the RAS; $return pops it. A branch increment is -2 to 1, and not allowed with a float test type.

docs.title: Encodings
docs.text:
The field layouts, as the reference assembler writes them (bit 31 is the bundle start bit, bits [30:26] the opcode):

Instruction Opcode Fields ALU 0x04-0x0F type[25:21] rd[20:16] rs1[15:11] imm-flag[10] rs2[4:0] or imm10[9:0] VALU (ALU) vector type, replicate[10] FSQRT 0x10 type rd rs1 DOT 0x11 type rd rs1 accumulate[10] rs2 CAST 0x12 dest type[25:21] rd source type[14:10] rs2 LOAD, STORE 0x13, 0x14 type rd rs1 imm-flag[10] incr[9:5] rs2, or imm10[9:0] SET 0x15 byte index[23:21] rd value[15:0] VREDUCE 0x16 type rd rs1 operation[10:6] (an ALU opcode) CMOV 0x17 type rd rs1 cond[10:8] incr[7:6] rs2 PACK 0x18 rd log2(P)[15:12] log2(W)[11:9] rs2 SLICE 0x19 high[5:1] in [25:21], rd, high[0] in [15], low[14:9], rs2 BRANCH 0x02 type[25:22] cond[21:19] incr[18:17] offset12[16:5] rs2 CALL 0x01 label-flag[25], offset25[24:0] or rs2 RETURN, NULL, HALT 0x03, 0x1A, 0x1B

ALU opcodes: + 0x04, - 0x05, * 0x06, / 0x07, | 0x08, & 0x09, ^ 0x0A, ~| 0x0B, ~& 0x0C, ~^ 0x0D, << 0x0E, >> 0x0F. Type codes: $i4..$i64 0x00-0x04, $u4..$u64 0x05-0x09, $f4..$f64 0x0A-0x0E, $u128 0x0F, $u256 0x10, $vu4..$vu32 0x11-0x14, $vf4..$vf32 0x15-0x18, $vi4..$vi32 0x19-0x1C.

docs.title: Writing and Running APARA Programs
docs.text: The apara configuration is one engine on its own: its program and data are placed straight into IMEM and DMEM (and its registers set) before the run, and the run ends when every thread it started has stopped. It comes, like every configuration, as a fast functional model (cpp_model) and a cycle-level timing model (sitar_model), with the same command line.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
model/system_models/apara/cpp_model/build.sh      # executable/apara_sim_cpp
model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/build.sh    # executable/apara_sim_sitar (needs sitar)

docs.title: Running a program
docs.text:
python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py prog.mcode
model/system_models/apara/cpp_model/executable/apara_sim_cpp \
        -p 0x0 -i prog.obj -d data.map -a registers.txt -r results.txt
Option Meaning -p <pc> start a thread at <pc> (hex, a word index); repeat for threads 1, 2, 3 (default: one thread at 0) -i <file> the object file -d <file> initial DMEM contents -a <file> initial register values -r <file> the expected final state: the run prints PASS or the mismatches and FAIL --dump-results <file> write the final state as a results file (- for the screen) --stats per-thread counts (cpp_model); the pipeline's counters (sitar_model) --trace print every bundle executed (cpp_model) --max-bundles <n> / --max-cycles <n> stop a run that does not end (cpp_model / sitar_model) --latency-file <file> instruction latencies (sitar_model, Ref Timing Model)

These are the options of the APARA reference simulator, mcode_run, plus ours, so the same files run on both. The exit status is 0 for PASS (or, without -r, when no thread stopped on an exception), 1 otherwise.

--trace shows the program as it runs:

t0 0x0:  ? ($i64) $r1 > --1 $goto pc+0;  + $r2 ($i64) $r2 $r1;  -> 0x0
t0 0x0:  ? ($i64) $r1 > --1 $goto pc+0;  + $r2 ($i64) $r2 $r1;
t0 0x8:  ? ($f32) $r3 < $goto pc+16;  -> 0x18
t0 0x18:  ? ($i16) $r4 < $goto pc+16;  + $r5 ($i64) $r0 1;  -> 0x28
t0 0x28:  $call pc+32;  + $r10 ($i64) $r0 16;  -> 0x48

(the end of a loop, from validation/apara/tests/control.mcode: a line per bundle, its thread and address, its instructions without the $nulls, and where it went if not to the next bundle).

A thread that stops on an exception is reported with its slot and cause:

thread 1: stopped at 0x8 by an exception: slot 4 unaligned memory address;

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
validation/apara/ holds the engine's tests: tests/ (one per instruction class, multithreading, bundle semantics, and the deviations) and timing/ (microbenchmarks with hand-derived cycle counts). Each test is one mcode file that also says how to run it and what to expect, in //@ lines:

// $cmov: if $rs2 satisfies the condition, $rd = $rs1.
//@ reg: 0 $r1 5
//@ expect: 0 reg $r4 0x5
//@ cycles: 7
    || $cmov ($i64) $r1 == $r4 $r2 ;
    || $halt ;
Line Meaning //@ threads: 0x0 0x20 start threads at these PCs (default: one at 0x0) //@ data: 10: 0x... an initial DMEM dword //@ reg: 0 $r3 0x10 an initial register: thread, register, value //@ expect: 0 reg $r5 0x7 an expected result (results-file format, registers as $rN) //@ cycles: 12 the exact cycle count on the timing model //@ deviation: <why> the test depends on a deviation from the reference model 
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py                 # all tests, cpp_model
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py --sitar         # on the timing model (also checks cycles)
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py validation/apara/timing --sitar
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py --reference --mcode-run <path to mcode_run>

The runner assembles each test, writes its files into validation/apara/build/<test>/, runs it, and prints PASS/FAIL. --reference also replays every test without a deviation line on the APARA reference simulator: ours writes its final state (PC, all registers, all of DMEM that is or was non-zero) as a results file, and the reference must reach exactly that state. This checks our model and the test's expectations at once.

docs.title: The APARA Engine in a System (sparc_apara)
docs.text: The sparc_apara configuration puts one APARA engine next to the SPARC core of core_l1cache_mmu_devices (with its L1 caches, MMU, and peripheral devices), as the APARA hardware attaches to an AJIT processor: the SPARC loads the engine's program, starts its threads and learns when they stop, and moves data in and out, all through memory- mapped registers; the engine can also read and write the system's memory itself.

docs.title: Address map
docs.text:
The system's physical addresses follow the AJIT_APARA layout (Ref model/cpp_common_code/SystemAddressMap.h), with the APARA parameter template's addresses for engine 0 of cluster 0:

Range What 0x0000_0000 .. main memory (256 MB), except: 0x0100_0000 .. 0x0100_FFFF the engine's DMEM, 64 KB 0xFFFE_0000 .. 0xFFFE_007F the engine's control unit (CCU) registers 0xFFFE_2000 .. 0xFFFE_207F the engine's DMA registers 0xFFFF_0000 .. 0xFFFF_FFFF the peripheral devices

Only main memory is ever cached; the engine's windows never are. A SPARC program should reach them with MMU-bypass accesses (ASI 0x20), as the routines below do. A program's own code and data must stay clear of the DMEM window.

Inside the engine, an address in its own DMEM window is local; every other address goes off island, to the system (the hardware's rule). So an engine program in a system addresses its DMEM by the window's address, usually through a register the host sets:

// $r9 = 0x01000000 (set by the SPARC): DMEM byte 0x100 is $r9 + 256.
    || $st ($i64) [$r9 + 256] $r3 ;

(The standalone apara configuration instead aliases every address into DMEM, as the APARA reference model does.)

docs.title: The control unit
docs.text:
Each thread has 8 32-bit registers at 0xFFFE_0000 + 32*thread + 4*register:

Register Contents R0 control: [31:16] sequence number, [15:14] thread (for command 9), [11:8] command, flags [4] run the command interpreter, [3] interrupt enable, [2] completed, [1] started, [0] start R1 PC R2 IMEM index / register index R3 IMEM write data / timer high R4 IMEM read data / timer low R5 completion: [31] valid, [26] RAS error, [25] halt, [24] exception, [23:0] exception codes R6 register high / stop PC / RAS depth R7 register low / next PC / RAS top

The host writes the arguments, then R0 with a command, start and run the command interpreter; the unit sets started, carries the command out, writes its results, and sets completed.

Command Does 1 read IMEM R4 := IMEM[R2] 2 write IMEM IMEM[R2] := R3 (IMEM is shared by the threads) 3 reset stop the thread: PC 0, RAS and ERROR cleared, registers kept 4 run start the thread at R1 5 read register R6:R7 := register R2 (high:low) 6 write register register R2 := R6:R7 7 completion once the thread has stopped: R5 := valid + its ERROR, R6 := its PC (each stop reported once); else R5 := 0. With interrupt enable, the command waits for the stop and then raises the engine interrupt 8 step run one bundle at R1, with local data only; R7 := the next PC 9 RAS state R6 := depth, R7 := top of thread R0[15:14]'s RAS 10 timer R3:R4 := the engine's cycle count

Writing R0 with interrupt enable clear clears the interrupt.

docs.title: The DMA unit
docs.text:
Four channels of 8 registers at 0xFFFE_2000 + 32*channel + 4*register:

Register Contents R0 control: [31:24] operation (1 load: system memory to DMEM; 2 store: DMEM to system memory), [23:20] and [19:16] the top 4 bits of the 36-bit source and destination, [15:8] sequence number, flags [4] error, [3] interrupt enable, [2] completed, [1] started, [0] scheduled R1, R2 source and destination base addresses R3 total bytes (for the record) R4 number of bursts R5 gap: the distance between bursts R6 bytes per burst; the stop cycle, once completed R7 the start cycle

Writing R0 with scheduled starts the channel. A load gathers: burst i comes from source + i·gap and lands at destination + i·(bytes per burst); a store scatters, the reverse. The DMEM side's address may be a DMEM offset or a window address. On completion: completed, and the interrupt if enabled; writing R0 with interrupt enable clear clears it. An unknown operation completes at once with error.

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text:
The engine's interrupt (its control unit's or its DMA unit's) drives the Interrupt Controller's external input, IRL 14. A handler for it, with the AJIT dispatch scheme of compiler/include/ajit_mt_irc.h:

void engine_handler(void)
{
    completion = apara_thread_completion(0);
    apara_clear_interrupt(0);
}
...
ajit_set_interrupt_handler(EXTERNAL_IRL, engine_handler);
writeInterruptControlRegister(0, 0, (1u << EXTERNAL_IRL) | 1u);
apara_start_thread(0, KERNEL_START);
apara_request_completion_interrupt(0);

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
compiler/include/apara_access_routines.h has the routines, in the style of AJIT's access routines:

Routine Does apara_load_program(words, n) IMEM words 0..n-1 apara_write_thread_register(t, r, v), apara_read_thread_register(t, r) a thread's 64-bit register apara_start_thread(t, pc), apara_reset_thread(t) apara_poll_thread(t), apara_wait_thread(t) the completion word apara_thread_stop_pc(t) where it stopped apara_request_completion_interrupt(t), apara_thread_completion(t), apara_clear_interrupt(t) completion by interrupt apara_dma_start(...), apara_dma_wait(c), apara_dma_load(c, dmem, src, n), apara_dma_store(c, dst, dmem, n) DMA apara_dmem_write_word(o, v), apara_dmem_read_word(o) DMEM directly, through the window apara_read_timer()

An engine program travels inside the SPARC program as a C array: compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py kernel.mcode writes kernel.mcode.h with kernel_program[], KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS, and a KERNEL_<LABEL> address for each label. A test's .vprj can name its kernels with MCODE = kernel.mcode lines; validation/build_hex.py then writes the headers before compiling.

A complete offload, from validation/C/apara/dma_dot_product/:

apara_load_program(kernel_program, KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS);
apara_dma_start(0, APARA_DMA_LOAD, (uint32_t) a, 0, 1, 0, N, 0);    // a -> DMEM 0
apara_dma_start(1, APARA_DMA_LOAD, (uint32_t) b, 256, 1, 0, N, 0);  // b -> DMEM 256
apara_dma_wait(0);
apara_dma_wait(1);
apara_write_thread_register(0, 9, APARA_DMEM_BASE);
apara_write_thread_register(0, 10, APARA_DMEM_BASE + 256);
apara_start_thread(0, KERNEL_START);
apara_wait_thread(0);
apara_dma_store(2, (uint32_t) result, 504, 8);                      // DMEM 504 -> result

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
cpp_model. AparaSystemCore (model/cpp_common_code/apara/) joins the engine (AparaCore), AparaControlCore and AparaDmaCore. The SystemBus routes the engine's windows to it; its off-island accesses and DMA transfers go back through the same bus. After every core cycle the engine runs one bundle and its DMA moves one piece (up to 8 bytes).

sitar_model. The engine's pipeline (AparaEngine, Ref Timing Model) and its host side (AparaHost: the control and DMA units) are sibling modules of the core, on a SystemInterconnect with two masters (the core and AparaHost, round robin):

Module Owns, does engine.exec the engine's state; serves host's requests on its service port (DMEM, registers, IMEM, thread commands), one cycle each; sends a bundle's off-island transactions to host and holds the bundle until they are answered; tells host when a thread stops host the CCU and DMA registers and commands; the engine's slave port (the SPARC's accesses to the three windows) and master port (DMA transfers, off-island accesses) interconnect one transaction at a time, from the core or the host, to main memory, the devices or the host

Every net crossing takes a cycle, so a SPARC access to a CCU register crosses four nets, and to DMEM six (through EXEC).

docs.title: APARA Timing Model
docs.text: The sitar_model of the apara configuration is a cycle-level model of the engine's pipeline, built from the APARA microarchitecture document (APARA Engine: Microarchitecture and Timing, in the APARA repository's engine_isp/docs/microarch). As everywhere in this project, the functionality comes from the same C++ class the fast model uses (AparaCore), and the timing from the Sitar structure itself: the pipeline's stages are modules, its channels are nets, and a bundle's time is spent waiting in them, never computed after the fact.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    F["FETCH<br/>(BTB, thread PCs)"] --> D["DECODE"]
    D -->|"4 channels,<br/>one per thread"| R["REGFILE<br/>(locks, tokens)"]
    R --> E["EXEC<br/>(AparaCore)"]
    E -->|results| R
    R --> W["WRITEBACK"]
    W -->|"PC correction,<br/>halt"| F

AparaEngine (model/sitar_component_models/AparaEngine.sitar) holds five modules, one per stage, joined by nets with the hardware's channel depths (2 entries, 1 for EXEC's results and WRITEBACK's notices). Each module pulls its inputs in phase 0 of a cycle and pushes its outputs in phase 1, so a bundle takes at least one cycle per stage, and a stage whose output channel is full holds its bundle: the hardware's elastic pipeline.

Stage Module What it does in a cycle FETCH AparaFetch picks a running thread (round robin), reads the 8-word IMEM line holding its PC, and sends the line's bundles one per cycle, in PC order, before picking another thread; predicts each bundle's next PC with the BTB DECODE AparaDecode decodes a bundle: registers read and written, latency, divider use; sends it on its thread's channel REGFILE AparaRegfile holds one bundle per thread; issues one per cycle (round robin) whose registers are all unlocked, if a token is free; locks the registers it writes. Releases a bundle's locks and token when its result comes back from EXEC EXEC AparaExec runs the bundle (AparaCore::step()) and holds it for its latency; skips wrong-path bundles WRITEBACK AparaWriteback sends FETCH a PC correction for a mispredicted bundle, a halt notice for a stopped thread

A bundle with no stalls is fetched in cycle c, decoded in c+1, issued in c+2, runs in EXEC from c+3, comes back to REGFILE after its latency and leaves WRITEBACK a cycle later: a one-bundle program takes 6 cycles.

docs.title: Timing rules
docs.text:
Latency. A bundle's time in EXEC is its slowest instruction's latency, from a table loaded at start-up (below), or its memory phase if that is longer. The defaults are the microarchitecture document's table:

Entry Cycles Covers nop any, control any, halt any, misc any, logic any 1 $null, branches/calls/returns, $halt, $set $slice $pack, | & ^ ~| ~& ~^ arith int<=32, arith fp<=16 1 + - * scalar and vector arith int64 2 arith fp32, arith fp64 3 shift int<=32 / shift int64 1 / 2 << >> dot int<=32, dot fp<=16 / dot int64, dot fp32, dot fp64 2 / 3 cast narrow / cast wide 1 / 2 narrow: integer to integer, float to integer, floats up to f16 vreduce any 2 assumed: not in the hardware's table cmov any 1 assumed: not in the hardware's table memory local 3 a bundle's DMEM accesses divide any, sqrt any 10 the designer's figure, to be confirmed

--latency-file <file> overrides entries, one <class> <operands> <cycles> per line (# comments):

arith fp32 5     # an f32 add/subtract/multiply takes 5 cycles
divide any 20

Memory. DMEM has two banks (address bit 15), each with one 256-bit port. A bundle's accesses to different banks proceed in parallel; accesses to the same bank one after another, each extra one adding bankConflictCycles (1).

Divider. / and $fsqrt share one unit: a bundle that needs it waits in EXEC until the previous user has finished.

EXEC. By default EXEC takes a new bundle every cycle (it is internally pipelined) and results leave it in order, one per cycle.

Register locks and tokens. A bundle waits in REGFILE while any register it reads or writes is locked by an earlier bundle of its thread. At most 2 bundles are in EXEC at a time (REGFILE's tokens); a token comes back with the bundle's result, two cycles after issue for a 1-cycle bundle, so the pipeline runs at one bundle per cycle.

Branch prediction. The branch target buffer has 256 entries, direct mapped by the low 8 bits of the bundle's PC and shared by the threads. Each holds a 22-bit tag, a 2-bit counter (0 strongly taken, 3 strongly not taken) and a target; a lookup predicts the target if the tag matches and the counter is below 3, otherwise the next bundle. Only PC corrections train it: a taken correction lowers the counter and sets the target, a not-taken one raises it, a new entry starts at 0 or 3.

Mispredicts. EXEC compares each bundle's actual next PC with FETCH's prediction. On a mismatch, the thread's state in EXEC becomes mispredicted: its following bundles, fetched on the wrong path, are skipped (not executed; their locks are still released) until FETCH, corrected by WRITEBACK, sends the first bundle of the right path, marked new stream. The penalty is 5 cycles with one thread; other threads keep the pipeline busy meanwhile. A halting bundle does the same for its thread, for good.

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text:
In model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/src/Top.sitar, one place for all of them (rebuild after a change):

Knob Default Meaning engine.fetch.imemDelay 0 cycles between picking a thread and its IMEM line arriving engine.exec.pipelined true false: EXEC holds one bundle for its whole latency engine.exec.latency.bankConflictCycles 1 per extra same-bank access in a bundle engine.regfile.tokens 2 bundles allowed in EXEC

--stats prints the pipeline's counters: bundles fetched, executed and skipped, mispredicts, BTB-predicted fetches, cycles lost to register locks, tokens and the divider, and bank conflicts.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
validation/apara/timing/ holds microbenchmarks, each with its cycle count derived by hand from the rules above and written in its header: one bundle (6 cycles), a stream at full rate, latency, a read-after-write stall versus the independent case, the shared divider, a bank conflict versus two banks, a mispredict, two threads. run_tests.py --sitar checks every count exactly. Each knob was also checked by changing it alone: every count moved by exactly the derived amount (for example imemDelay = 1 adds one cycle per IMEM line, tokens = 1 halves the issue rate).

The model is checked against the microarchitecture document, not yet against the hardware (Aa_model) traces: its open items (the latencies marked above, EXEC's structure, same-bank ordering) are listed in Deviations and Findings.

docs.title: log_viewer/
docs.text: A lightweight, self-contained, single-file browser tool for viewing SPARC V8 instruction/state traces produced by CoreLogger (model/cpp_common_code/CoreLogger.h) -- used by every configuration's cpp_model and sitar_model, since both drive the same SparcCore and therefore emit the same trace format.

docs.title: What's here
docs.text:
• viewer.html -- the viewer itself. A single HTML file, no build step, no external dependencies (works entirely offline, nothing is fetched from the network). Open it directly in any modern browser.
  • test_simple_ADD.log / test_simple_ADD.objdump -- symlinks to a small sample trace and its matching disassembly, generated from the bundled test_simple_ADD example (see below and ../validation/README.md), so you can explore the viewer without building or running anything first. Named to match, not sim_trace.*, so it's the same file the walkthroughs elsewhere produce, not a differently-named copy.

docs.title: Trace format
docs.text: Tab-separated, one row per architectural event (FETCH, TRAP_RAISED, TRAP_ENTER, MEM_READ, MEM_WRITE, ATOMIC, RESET, ANNUL, HALT, or a generic one-off): seq, time, pc, event, detail, followed by the entire current-window processor state (PSR fields named and in binary, general registers in hex). See CoreLogger.h for exactly what each event logs and why. The viewer only requires seq/time/pc/ event/detail to be present -- any extra columns a future trace source adds are simply ignored, not required.

docs.title: Viewing a trace
docs.text:
1. Build the cpp model with logging enabled, and run a test program: 
    model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex
    This writes test_simple_ADD.log into the current directory (a trace file is always named after the hex file it ran).
  2. Open log_viewer/viewer.html in a browser (double-click it, or open log_viewer/viewer.html / xdg-open log_viewer/viewer.html).
  3. Click Load trace and pick test_simple_ADD.log; click Load objdump and pick validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.objdump (the matching disassembly, see ../validation/README.md).

docs.title: Example: viewing the bundled test_simple_ADD example
docs.text:
From the repository root:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex
open log_viewer/viewer.html   # or: xdg-open log_viewer/viewer.html

Then in the viewer: Load trace -> test_simple_ADD.log (written into the repository root, since that's where the command above was run from), Load objdump -> validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.objdump.

docs.title: The same, via the sitar model
docs.text:
model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/executable/sparc_sim_sitar_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.expected

Writes test_simple_ADD.log (sparcThread's trace, directly loadable, same as above) and sitar.log (everything else Sitar logs -- see model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/README.md) into the current directory.

docs.title: Optional: serve it for auto-loading
docs.text:
If you'd rather not click through file pickers every time, serve the directory containing both files and pass them as URL query parameters -- the viewer fetch()es them automatically on load:

cd log_viewer
python3 -m http.server 8000

then open http://localhost:8000/viewer.html?trace=test_simple_ADD.log (the bundled sample -- the viewer also automatically tries the same basename with a .objdump extension, test_simple_ADD.objdump here). For a freshly generated trace, copy it (and its .objdump) into this directory first, or point ?trace= at a relative path if your server root already covers both files. This only works over http(s), not a plain file:// URL -- browsers block a page from reading another local file just by name.

docs.title: Using the viewer
docs.text:
• Search: field=value (e.g. PC=0x1c, l4=0x3434, T=56) matches a specific column; plain text with no = searches every column for a substring.
  • prev / next: step through search matches only. Use the Up/Down arrow keys to step through the trace row by row regardless of search.
  • Click a row in the Trace panel to select it and see its state. Click a line in Disassembly to jump to the first trace row at that address.
  • The Trace panel's event column is colored by event type (e.g. FETCH amber, EXECUTED green, the two trap events orange, HALT red, RESET purple, memory events blue), so a given kind of row is easy to pick out while scanning.
  • All three panels (Disassembly, Trace, State) are independently resizable -- drag the thin dividers between them.
  • Light/dark theme toggle, top right.
